items.label: f03-three-values-per-field
items.front: Stale-edit review: what state do you need to tell 'fields the other writer changed' from 'fields I changed'?
items.back: Three values per field: the snapshot the editor opened with, the draft, and the latest saved row. A field conflicts only when both sides moved away from the snapshot - so keep the opening snapshot in its own state.

items.label: f01-password-change-recovery
items.front: Password change revokes the current session in the same transaction. Why can't the client simply replay its receipt after a lost response, and what simple flow is acceptable?
items.back: The revoked session can no longer authenticate the replay. A documented flow: sign in again with the new password, and if that fails (outcome uncertain) with the old one. Do not promise ordinary receipt replay unless the design supports it.

items.label: f04-optional-text-null
items.front: Why does HrisRules.OptionalText map whitespace-only input to null instead of using input.Description?.Trim()?
items.back: So 'absent' has exactly one representation in the database. Trim() would store "" for a blank form, a second way to mean 'no description'; delegating to Text keeps the length rule in one place.

items.label: f02-refund-concurrency-vs-retry
items.front: Refunds: how should two different operation keys competing for one refund differ from a retry of the same key?
items.back: Different keys: one wins, the other observes the closed state or a uniqueness constraint. Same key: recover the already committed result. A version protects stale intent but does not replace refund uniqueness.

items.prompt: Jordan signs in as HR at 09:00 with an eight-hour JWT; an Admin demotes Jordan at 09:10. What does Jordan's next request see, and why?

choices.text: A 401 on every request, because any role change revokes all of Jordan's tokens
Full HR access until 17:00, because the role is signed into the eight-hour JWT
HR access until Jordan reloads the browser page and fetches a new token
The demotion, because each request reloads the current session, account and role from the database

choices: A 401 on every request, because any role change revokes all of Jordan's tokens
Full HR access until 17:00, because the role is signed into the eight-hour JWT
HR access until Jordan reloads the browser page and fetches a new token
The demotion, because each request reloads the current session, account and role from the database

items.explanation: The token carries stable account/session identity; authorization reads current state, so the next request observes the change. Logout deletes the server session too.

items.prompt: PTO hours are stored as quarter-hour integers. A 120-hour balance has a 7.75-hour request deducted. What is stored, and what happens to a 0.1-hour request?

choices.text: 112 units; 0.1 hours is rounded up to one quarter-hour
449 units (112.25 hours); 0.1 hours is rejected
449 units; 0.1 hours is rounded down to zero and accepted
11225 units; 0.1 hours is stored as zero units

choices: 112 units; 0.1 hours is rounded up to one quarter-hour
449 units (112.25 hours); 0.1 hours is rejected
449 units; 0.1 hours is rounded down to zero and accepted
11225 units; 0.1 hours is stored as zero units

items.explanation: 120 h = 480 units, 7.75 h = 31 units, 480 - 31 = 449. Values that are not whole quarter-hours are refused instead of rounded silently.

items.prompt: What distinct problems do record versions and operation receipts solve?

choices.text: Receipts replace versions entirely once idempotency keys are enabled
Versions recover lost responses; receipts detect concurrent edits
Versions detect stale intent; receipts recover one intent's outcome
Both prevent duplicates; a receipt is just the HTTP name for a version

choices: Receipts replace versions entirely once idempotency keys are enabled
Versions recover lost responses; receipts detect concurrent edits
Versions detect stale intent; receipts recover one intent's outcome
Both prevent duplicates; a receipt is just the HTTP name for a version

items.explanation: They are complementary: a stale edit is detected by the version; a lost response is recovered by replaying the same key.

It would silently overwrite Jordan's change instead of letting Maya review it
Strong ETags cannot be refreshed while an unsaved draft exists in the editor
The server would reject the resend, because the operation key was already used

choices: It would lose Maya's draft, because the draft is stored inside the old ETag
It would silently overwrite Jordan's change instead of letting Maya review it
Strong ETags cannot be refreshed while an unsaved draft exists in the editor
The server would reject the resend, because the operation key was already used

items.explanation: A version protects intent. After review the user may keep the draft and retry with the latest version; the server stays authoritative.

items.prompt: An HR user edits an employee and includes accountRole in the request body. What happens?

choices.text: Rejected: HR cannot set account roles in employee requests
Applied, since HR manages all ordinary employee data
Queued as a pending role change for an Admin to approve
Ignored silently, and the remaining fields are saved

choices: Rejected: HR cannot set account roles in employee requests
Applied, since HR manages all ordinary employee data
Queued as a pending role change for an Admin to approve
Ignored silently, and the remaining fields are saved

items.explanation: A business title (JobRole) is not a security role. Only Admin creates or changes accounts; HR also cannot edit an Admin employee.

items.prompt: Why does Nethris open an immediate SQLite write transaction before reading the PTO balance it will change?

choices.text: Immediate transactions bypass the WAL file, which makes each approval faster
It lets other readers see the uncommitted balance deduction early
It reserves the write lock before reading, so concurrent approvers take turns
It lets EF SaveChanges commit every write as soon as that write is made

choices: Immediate transactions bypass the WAL file, which makes each approval faster
It lets other readers see the uncommitted balance deduction early
It reserves the write lock before reading, so concurrent approvers take turns
It lets EF SaveChanges commit every write as soon as that write is made

items.explanation: With an outer transaction, SaveChanges is not the final commit; the API owns one durable outcome for state, hours and history.

items.prompt: A client reuses an operation key but sends a different body. What does Nethris return?

choices.text: The recorded result of the first request, since the operation key matches
A fresh execution of the new body, stored under the same operation key
A conflict, because the stored fingerprint for that key no longer matches
A 428, because the If-Match header must change whenever the body changes

choices: The recorded result of the first request, since the operation key matches
A fresh execution of the new body, stored under the same operation key
A conflict, because the stored fingerprint for that key no longer matches
A 428, because the If-Match header must change whenever the body changes

items.explanation: Same key plus same fingerprint replays the recorded result; same key plus different content is a conflict. Receipts are scoped to account and key, kept 24 hours.
